Oct 8 : Spotify said on Thursday it had signed a new multiyear licensing agreement with podcaster Joe Rogan for "The Joe Rogan Experience", extending a partnership that began in 2020. The renewal has similar terms to Rogan's previous deal, which carried an estimated earnout of $250 million, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Spotify did not disclose financial terms and did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. The show debuted in 2009 and was exclusive to Spotify from 2020 until the 2024 renewal, when it also became available on Apple, Amazon and YouTube. Spotify said new episodes would keep coming out each week on its platform and elsewhere.

Oct 8 : FIFA President Gianni Infantino promised further resources for Africa as he addressed football association presidents at a conference in Cape Verde on Thursday, a rare public speech since his bid to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments collapsed in July. Infantino had to shelve his plan, which included selling a stake in the World Cup, after a backlash from mostly European and North American nations, many of which have withdrawn support for him at next year’s presidential elections. All presidents of the Confederation of African Football's 54 associations were due to attend the conference, a first-of-its-kind strategy symposium for African football, which provided a platform for Swiss-Italian Infantino to address more than a quarter of the voters ahead of next year’s FIFA elections. He reminded the CAF presidents of the financial contribution FIFA has made to African football since he was elected in 2016.

"As FIFA president, I am proud to have contributed with you a little bit in this revolution (in African football) in the last 10 years," Infantino said. "With the FIFA Forward programme we have invested one billion dollars in 10 years in Africa, with 124 different projects and many other actions." Without referring directly to the failed bid to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments, Infantino spoke of wanting an open dialogue on matters of disagreement. "When you go through a journey, sometimes concerns are raised," he said. "When they are raised, we have to address them. As far as we are concerned at FIFA, we address them always with the spirit of dialogue and with open arms, an open heart and an open mind. We can always be better and do better." He reiterated his support for Africa and that FIFA would continue to invest in the continent. "Our commitment is to make sure that your football is going to continue to improve and grow, give you more opportunities. Ten countries at the (last) World Cup has been a success for the entire continent," he said. "We need to continue together on this path, because it is up to you as CAF to tell us what you want. How we can make you stronger and better. "We will continue to look for the resources and the increases (in funding) that are necessary to boost the African game to the top of world football."

Source: Reuters

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 8 : Amazon on Thursday unveiled a slate of higher-end tablets that for the first time feature its Alexa+ voice assistant and run on Google's Android operating system, a bet that consumers will pay more for premium devices after years of focusing on the budget end of the market. Seattle-based Amazon had been working on the tablets under the code name Kittyhawk, as Reuters reported exclusively last year, to transition away from its more limited homegrown Fire OS operating system software, after years of gripes from consumers and app developers. Fire OS is a “forked” version of Android, with modifications to make it work like a unique operating system. Known as Alexa Tablets, the line features several different versions with starting prices from $230 to $500; all are made with aluminum cases, a switch from Fire tablets’ plastic. The new tablets will cost as much as $550, a big bump from Amazon’s more recent top-of-the-line Fire HD 10 tablet which cost upwards of $180, though the company often discounted them.

The top Alexa tablet, with 128 gigabytes of memory, for $550 compares with an Apple iPad for $450 and Samsung's Galaxy tablet for $550. The product revamp marks a new strategy under devices chief Panos Panay to move upscale and away from the inexpensive gadgets Amazon sold at or near cost to hook customers into using Prime Video, Kindle, music apps and the main e-commerce website. That focus on affordability came with compromises, like lower screen quality and battery life, compared with rivals Apple and Samsung and others. Alexa+, an advanced AI-powered version of the Alexa voice assistant, will feature prominently on the devices to help perform actions or answer questions using generative AI. Accessing Alexa+ on the tablets will require a Prime membership or Alexa+ subscription, Amazon said. Amazon is pushing the pricier devices as worldwide tablet sales are falling, down 12 per cent in the second quarter from the year before to 33.6 million units, according to IDC data. The US market, which has been especially hurt by a shortage of memory chips, saw sales plunge 32 per cent in the second quarter year over year, IDC data showed. The Seattle company held just 1.9 per cent of the global tablet market in this year’s second quarter, down from 8 per cent a year earlier, according to IDC. Apple is the leader with 34 per cent, followed by Samsung at 17.5 per cent. The tablet prices do not include a one-time fee customers have to pay to turn off advertising displayed on the lockscreen, though the highest-priced Alexa Tablet will not have the ads. It will require a one-time $20 fee to eliminate the ads, up from $15 for Fire OS tablets, a spokesperson said. Such ads help users “discover new content that’s relevant to their interests” and the revenue helps underwrite other innovations, the spokesperson said. UPGRADE FROM FIRE OS With Android, Alexa Tablet customers won’t be limited to the apps offered in the Fire OS app store, disdained by developers who had to make a third version of apps offered in the Google Play and Apple stores. And the built-in Alexa+ voice AI assistant helps to differentiate the tablets from others. Amazon has spent billions overhauling Alexa to power it with generative AI and make it more capable for connected homes, shopping and accessing third-party services like Uber and Grubhub. The service, free with a Prime membership, is unprofitable. Prior Fire OS tablets will still work, said the spokesperson, but she did not say whether Amazon will continue to maintain the operating system or app store. Earlier this year Amazon cut off support for older Kindle models, citing software maintenance costs as a reason.

Source: Reuters

AMSTERDAM, Oct 8 : A successor to ASML's most advanced chipmaking machine could be ready in about 10 years, engineers for the company and its optics partner Carl Zeiss said in a peer-reviewed paper. The tool, dubbed "Hyper NA", would print smaller circuitry while re-using much of the companies' existing technology, the paper said, though challenges remain. The machine, which ASML has begun developing but has not committed to producing, matters for the company's future prospects, as well as those of its partners and competitors.  ASML had no immediate comment.

The company is Europe's most valuable by market capitalization, thanks to its monopoly on lithography tools that use extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light to print the tiny circuitry of AI chips. SMALLER, FASTER CHIPS The paper in the October issue of the Journal of Micro/Nanopatterning, Materials and Metrology says Hyper NA could print features as small as 5 nanometers, more than a third smaller than ASML's current "High NA" EUV tool.  Though chipmakers are improving chips with 3-D designs, smaller features remain key for speed and power usage, and lithography is a limiting factor. Among chip manufacturers, Intel has begun using High NA in production, while last month Samsung and SK Hynix said they would follow in 2028 and TSMC in 2030. The paper said Zeiss can already make mirrors precise enough for Hyper NA, and the machine would be barely larger than High NA tools, already the size of a double-decker bus. Beyond Hyper NA, the authors said, tools would likely need to use a shorter wavelength of light, still a matter for academic research.  They said ASML's current light source "can be reused as is" for Hyper NA, while mentioning in a note that an alternative technique with free electron lasers would not change the lighting system's design. Those remarks are relevant for US startups including xLight, which is developing free-electron laser light sources that Elon Musk has hinted he might favor at his Terafab chip plant in Texas, and for Substrate, which is pursuing X-ray lithography.

Source: Reuters

LONDON, Oct 8 : The growth of women's soccer worldwide needs careful collaboration to make sure players are not overloaded by increasing competitions, National Women's Soccer League Commissioner Jessica Berman said on Wednesday.  FIFA's inaugural Women's Club World Cup is set to take place in January 2028, mid-season for Europe's top domestic leagues but in the close season for the NWSL. The new 19-team tournament is scheduled to take place six months after the Women's World Cup in Brazil, and with anterior cruciate ligament injuries still blighting the women's game, Berman stressed the need for mutual understanding among all parties involved to make sure players are not overworked.  "I think this next phase of growth really requires a ton of communication and collaboration between the different stakeholders, or tournament organisers, because we're all leveraging the same players for these different tournaments," Berman told reporters at the Leaders Week sports industry conference at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge stadium.

"And we must communicate to make sure that we're optimising for their performance in a way that allows for us all to have the longevity and sustainability that we're looking to achieve. "So, I think more details (are) to come from FIFA. We too are waiting for additional information about everything from the location to the format to the structure, and we will hope to continue to work with FIFA on making sure that it's curated in a way that supports the growth of the game globally." POTENTIAL HOSTING BOOST The Women's Club World Cup will have six teams in the play-in stage, with the three winners advancing to the group stage joining 13 other clubs. There will be four groups of four, with the top two teams from each progressing to the knockout stage. The AFC, CAF, CONCACAF and CONMEBOL confederations will each have two direct slots, while UEFA will have five berths.  While FIFA has not announced a host, British media reports this month said the US was in advanced talks to stage the tournament. Should that be the case, the NWSL could get a boost from it, Berman said.  "I think there's a lot of opportunity if it were to be hosted in America," she said.  "I think I'd want to hear more about what the plans would be, but certainly (with) that exposure there could be benefits for our league and so we'll continue to be available to discuss opportunities that might exist in our market." Defending NWSL champions Gotham, who will play in the Club World Cup, lead the 16-team league standings on 55 points, four ahead of San Diego, with three regular-season games remaining. The top eight teams contest the playoffs. Berman, who became commissioner in 2022, did not put an upper limit on the number of teams the league could expand to but said 20 would be the "next touch point".

Source: Reuters

MANCHESTER, Oct 8 : The Premier League resumes this weekend with one of its flagship fixtures, but Manchester City's trip to Liverpool will unfold amid a hostile atmosphere and beneath an unprecedented cloud following the club's guilty verdict in a landmark financial case. City head to Anfield on Sunday for their first league game since an independent commission found the club guilty of more than 100 serious breaches of the league's financial rules over nine years, as well as charges relating to their failure to co-operate with the investigation. "If they want an understanding of how angry the game is going to be, then Anfield will tell them like you would never believe," former Manchester United captain and England defender Gary Neville declared recently on The Overlap podcast. "I suspect there may be banners, there will certainly be chanting. There will be a reception like you have never seen for them at Anfield... it will be a brutal day."

City have appealed the decision and continue to maintain their innocence, saying the commission's opinion contains "clear material errors" and that they possess evidence supporting their position. For now, however, the legal battle and the football season occupy the same uneasy space. City have carried on imperiously on the pitch, winning all five of their league matches to start the campaign, and will arrive at Anfield looking to preserve that perfect record. Liverpool, meanwhile, have endured a less convincing opening, with two wins and three draws from their opening five league games. That would normally provide more than enough intrigue for a fixture between two clubs that have shaped much of the top flight's recent history, but events away from the pitch have transformed Sunday's game into something far bigger. SANCTIONS YET TO BE DETERMINED Every City appearance now comes with questions over what ultimately awaits the club, with the appeal process still to run and sanctions yet to be determined. The uncertainty has already prompted discussion over possible compensation claims from opposing teams and players and the broader consequences for English football. Anfield is hardly the gentlest place for City to return to domestic action after the international break. The rivalry between the clubs already carried plenty of edge after years of battles near the top of English football. Now Sunday's encounter will provide the first indication of how City's players handle the scrutiny generated by a verdict that reaches far beyond the usual rhythms of a title race. There is plenty at stake for sixth-placed Liverpool, too. Victory would provide an emphatic lift after their modest start and land the first blow on a City team who have so far been flawless. Defending champions Arsenal, who trail City by three points in second, kick off the weekend at home to Leeds United on Saturday. Mikel Arteta's side know victory would lift them provisionally level on points with Enzo Maresca's City. Leeds have provided one of the season's early surprises, sitting fifth after going unbeaten through five games. Another heavyweight fixture follows later on Saturday when Manchester United host Tottenham Hotspur, with both struggling sides desperate to inject some momentum into their seasons. United are 12th with just one victory, while Spurs are bottom with just two points. The meeting adds another layer of intrigue to a weekend already dominated by events at Anfield, with two traditional powers under pressure to turn around difficult starts when they meet at Old Trafford. Yet inevitably most eyes will be fixed on Anfield. After an unusually long pause in domestic football, the Premier League returns with its most contentious off-field controversy far from resolved.

Source: Reuters

DURBAN, Oct 8 : South Africa’s lead attack bowler Kagiso Rabada will sit out the first test against Australia, which starts in Durban on Friday, with the home side to field two spinners at Kingsmead. Rabada was in contention for selection as he worked his way back to fitness after a hamstring injury in June, and trained with the team at Kingsmead on Thursday but has been left out to continue his recovery, captain Temba Bavuma told a press conference. “It wasn’t an easy (decision). I think we did go the conservative route, to give him a couple of extra days to get closer to where he can be at 100 per cent fitness,” Bavuma said. Rabada would be in contention for the second test in Gqeberha, which starts on October 18, he added..

Oct 8 : Investor concerns that Nvidia-backed Firmus may cut the size of its $5 billion Australian initial public offering (IPO) drove a 30 per cent plunge in shares of construction services provider Maas Group, which owns 3.2 per cent in the AI data centre operator. The final details of Firmus' share sale, the second-largest ever in Australia, were still being finalised on Thursday, according to a person familiar with the matter. Firmus did not respond to a request for comment from Reuters. Sentiment towards AI has shifted sharply in recent weeks as concerns over high valuations have broadened to worries the technology is slipping out of human control and the prospect that massive technology spending may never pay off.

Firmus and its advisors on Thursday were contemplating cutting the size of the IPO and reducing the price per share from A$11 each to A$8.25, according to local media reports. Bookbuilding closed earlier Thursday and potential investors were told in a term sheet reviewed by Reuters "the joint active bookrunners will provide further information in relation to the offer." SOME INVESTORS SAY THEY ARE WARY OF VALUATION The deal's initial term sheet had said indicative offers for the IPO were already above the deal's size. But some potential investors told Reuters they were cautious about the company's burgeoning valuation, ability to execute on its ambitious growth plans and hefty debt pile. Demand for Firmus stock from overseas investors was weaker than expected for the IPO, the reports said, which was to be a landmark transaction for Australia's subdued capital markets. Shares of Maas closed down 22.4 per cent on Thurday, after falling much as 30 per cent in intraday trading, its weakest level since May 6. The company lost about A$517 million ($359.52 million) in market. It is valued at A$1.79 billion. Maas was questioned by the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) over the share price plunge. The company said in an exchange filing that speculation over whether the IPO would proceed had weighed on sentiment, adding it was not aware of any undisclosed information that would explain the trading "The selloff reflects a legitimate derating of the embedded value of its Firmus stake, but the magnitude is overdone," said Emanuel Ajay Datt, managing director of fund manager Datt Group. A cut in Firmus' offer price to A$9 from A$11 would reduce the value of Maas' holding by about A$75 million, Datt said, adding that the loss was modest relative to the company's market value decline on the day. Firmus' $5 billion IPO was to be Australia's largest new share sale in nearly three decades, behind only top telco Telstra's roughly $10 billion float in 1997. ($1 = 1.4380 Australian dollars)

Oct 8 : Technology companies and utilities are increasingly exploring ways to make power-hungry data centers more flexible in when and how they consume electricity, helping ease the strain on US power grids as AI-driven demand surges. The strategy, called "demand response", involves data centers temporarily reducing or shifting electricity use during periods of peak demand or grid stress, and is gaining traction as a way to reduce the need for costly grid upgrades and new power generation. It's a tool that states around the US, federal agencies and market operators are increasingly exploring, said Lauren Shwisberg, a principal at energy think tank RMI. WHY DOES DATA CENTER FLEXIBILITY MATTER?

US data center electricity use could rise from about 177 to 192 terawatt-hours in 2024 to between 383 and 793 TWh by 2030, according to the Electric Power Research Institute. Meanwhile, data centers surveyed by the group reported peak power reduction potential of 10 per cent to 30 per cent, depending on facility type, with some hyperscalers going even higher, according to Arin Kaye, EPRI technical leader. A study by Duke University's Nicholas Institute estimated that greater flexibility from data centers could save between $40 billion and $150 billion in capital investments over the next decade. It could also help data centers connect to the grid more quickly, as regulators and grid operators explore faster pathways for facilities willing to curb electricity use during periods of high demand. WHERE DO EFFORTS STAND? So far, the "demand response" strategy for data centers has mostly been deployed through pilot projects or one-off agreements. OpenAI, for example, recently agreed to cut the electricity it draws from the grid by up to 1 gigawatt from a planned 3.2-gigawatt facility in Georgia during periods of grid stress. This, however, is gradually evolving into a broader push. Federal regulators in June ordered grid operators to consider new rules for connecting large power users to the grid, including new pathways for facilities offering this flexibility to connect faster. Last month, Alphabet's Google, NVIDIA and Emerald AI launched an initiative called the AI Energy Management Alliance, aimed at advancing the deployment of "flexible" data centers. WHAT ARE THE KEY CHALLENGES? Experts say scaling up the strategy will require changes on both sides. Data centers need to figure out how to adjust power consumption without disrupting customers, while utilities and grid operators need to develop tariffs, market incentives and faster interconnection pathways that reward that flexibility. "Demand response can materially soften peak impacts, but scaling curtailment agreements across hundreds of new facilities will demand significant capital expenditure and coordinated policy frameworks," said Alexander Kheder, analyst with BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions.

Source: Reuters

Oct 8 : PepsiCo warned on Thursday that growth and margin recovery in its key North American market was taking longer than planned and said it would pursue additional cost cuts to offset sluggish demand for its snacks and beverages. Faced with high input costs, inflation hit to demand and the growing threat of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, the company is pursuing record productivity savings in its turnaround efforts launched after activist investor Elliott Investment Management took a roughly $4 billion stake a year ago. PepsiCo's third-quarter revenue exceeded market expectations and the company adjusted its 2026 organic revenue forecast to about 3 per cent from a prior view of 2 per cent to 4 per cent, but flagged slow progress and profitability struggles in North America. "In North America, we remain committed to improving growth and core operating margin," said CFO Steve Schmitt in prepared remarks. "However, it is taking more time than we planned. Therefore, we expect North America's core operating margin performance to remain under pressure in the fourth quarter."

PepsiCo's core operating margin dropped 35 basis points in the third quarter from a year ago and was down 25 basis points year to date at 16.5 per cent of revenue. In December, after discussions with Elliott, PepsiCo said it was targeting a 100-basis-point uptick over three years. The company also cut its fiscal 2026 forecast for core earnings per share after adjusting for currency fluctuations to an increase of 1 per cent to 2 per cent, compared with previous expectations for the low end of the 4 per cent to 6 per cent range. The challenge is industry-wide. Packaged food makers such as General Mills, McCormick and Conagra Brands are spending more on promotions and affordability initiatives to revive demand while contending with higher input costs. PepsiCo, whose shares were up about 1 per cent in early trading, is expanding its range of high-protein products to tackle the GLP-1 threat and is now promising extra productivity savings. "Additional structural cost reduction actions are being identified and will be implemented in the coming months to help fund investments that aim to accelerate organic revenue growth and mitigate the impacts of rising input cost inflation," CEO Ramon Laguarta said in a statement. PepsiCo's international business continues to perform well, but North America weakness, where third-quarter volumes in food were flat and dipped 2 per cent in beverages from a year ago, is a persistent pain point. "The beverage business continues to disappoint, and we expect PepsiCo will continue to be a source of share to both Coca-Cola and Keurig Dr Pepper." said Nik Modi, analyst at RBC Capital Markets. "PepsiCo will have to fully refranchise its beverage business or it will continue to lose share." The company cut prices by up to 15 per cent on products such as Lay's and Doritos in February, but last month said it would raise some chip prices to keep pace with input cost inflation. CEO Laguarta has bought some goodwill with the international numbers, but the pressure he is under is high and rising, said David Wagner, head of equity and portfolio manager at PepsiCo investor Aptus Capital Advisors, noting that patience from the board and activists is finite. "Next couple of quarters need to show real North American inflection, or the pressure moves from 'deliver the turnaround' to 'explain why you're still the right person to lead it'," he said.
